analysis.one_liner: Rewrites the federal prevailing-wage law for construction, exempting small contracts while tightening wage enforcement.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Sen. Kennedy in March 1993 and referred to the Senate labor committee, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote and died when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace the Davis-Bacon Act, the 1931 law requiring contractors on federal construction jobs to pay workers locally prevailing wages. It would exempt small contracts — up to $100,000 for new construction and $15,000 for renovations — from that requirement, but it would stop contractors from splitting a big project into small contracts to dodge coverage. On covered jobs, it would strengthen enforcement: wage determinations must use data no more than three years old, workers could sue, willful violators would owe double back pay plus attorney fees, and repeat violators could be barred from federal contracts for three to five years.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction workers on larger federal jobs would gain stronger wage enforcement, more current wage determinations, double damages for willful underpayment, and easier lawsuits with paid attorney fees. Contractors doing small federal jobs would also benefit, because contracts under the new dollar thresholds would no longer require prevailing wages or the related payroll paperwork.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Construction workers on large federal jobs

how_it_helps.text: On covered federal construction contracts, laborers and mechanics must be paid wages the Labor Secretary determines to be prevailing locally, and contractors may take contributions toward fringe benefits only up to the prevailing amount.

Contracts that individually fall under the dollar threshold but together exceed it, and relate to the same project, would be treated as a single contract, closing the loophole of splitting work into small pieces to avoid coverage.
Wage determinations must be based on data no more than three years old, and if no data exists the highest comparable prevailing wage in the state applies, keeping determinations current.

Workers and other interested people could bring civil actions for unpaid wages, with double payment plus attorney fees if the violation was willful, and could petition for review when an agency decides a contract is not covered.

Contractors who violate wage rules could face suspension of payments, withheld contract funds to cover unpaid wages, and debarment from federal contracts for three years (five for a repeat violation).
Federal law would not preempt stronger state, local, or tribal prevailing-wage requirements on federally financed construction.

analysis.who_pays: Workers on small federal contracts — under $100,000 for new construction or $15,000 for renovations — would lose prevailing-wage protection on those jobs. Covered contractors would bear tougher enforcement, monthly payroll reporting with suspension of payments for late reports, double damages for willful violations, and possible debarment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers on small jobs; covered contractors

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts new-construction contracts up to $100,000 and renovation, repair, and demolition contracts up to $15,000 from prevailing-wage requirements, removing that protection from workers on a large number of small federal jobs.
It allows 'helpers' to be paid below the prevailing rate where helper classifications are common in the area, opening a lower pay category on covered jobs.

It imposes heavier compliance duties on covered contractors, including three-year record retention, monthly certified payroll reports with automatic payment suspension for late filings, and posting of wage scales at work sites.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a genuine trade. Workers on large federal construction jobs would get meaningfully stronger wage protection — current wage data, double damages, employer burden of proof, and debarment. But workers on thousands of small federal jobs would lose prevailing-wage coverage entirely, and the lower-paid helper category slightly dilutes the standard on covered work. Whether it nets out well depends on how many jobs fall under the new dollar thresholds.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on March 22, 1993, read twice, and sent to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which never held a hearing or markup; it died there when the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced the bill on March 22, 1993 and spoke on it, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
One Democratic senator cosponsored the bill.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action appears in the record for the rest of the 103rd Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: the 1931-era Davis-Bacon law and its very low coverage threshold stayed as they were, small-contract contractors continued without the new exemptions they would have gained, and workers never received either the stronger enforcement or the small-job coverage loss.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: unchanged law, no new exemptions

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.role: Senator from Massachusetts and Chair, Senate Labor and Human Resources; introduced the bill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, delivered introductory remarks on it, and referred it to the committee he chaired, which never took it up.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; chaired by the bill's own sponsor
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the remainder of the 103rd Congress without a hearing, markup, or report.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. The sponsor and its sole cosponsor were both Democrats; there is no record of Republican positions on this particular bill.

industries.note: The bill exempts their small contracts from prevailing-wage rules and lets lower-paid helpers work on covered jobs, cutting labor costs. But on covered jobs it imposes double damages, payment suspension for late payroll reports, and three-to-five-year debarment for violators.

industries.industry: Building trades unions and organized labor
industries.note: Stronger enforcement, current wage data, and anti-contract-splitting rules would raise wages for members on large federal jobs, but the coverage exemptions would remove prevailing-wage protection from smaller jobs where union standards are weakest.
